overview.title: Hidden hypotheses, an ethics warning, and the start of data collection
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.main_topic: The two hypotheses implicit in framing an ML problem, the ethical dimension of task choice, and the cost of data collection
overview.central_idea: Framing a problem as 'predict targets Y from inputs X' rests on two unproven hypotheses (Y is predictable from X, and your data is informative enough to learn the mapping); some tasks should not be attempted at all for ethical reasons; and once the task is fixed, collecting and labeling data is usually the most expensive part of the project.
overview.importance: This page marks the hinge between thinking about a problem and committing resources to it. It warns that a well-framed task may still be unlearnable, that technical choices carry moral weight, and that the bulk of real project effort goes into data, not models.
learning_objectives: State the two hypotheses you implicitly make when you frame an ML problem as mapping inputs to targets.
Explain why assembling (X, Y) pairs does not guarantee that X carries enough information to predict Y, using the stock-price example.
Summarize the book's argument for why a 'trustworthiness from a face' model is both invalid and harmful.
Recognize data collection and annotation as the most arduous, time-consuming and costly part of most ML projects.
Describe the concrete data-collection needs of the photo-search and spam-detection example projects.
prerequisites: The example consulting projects introduced on p.195-196 (photo search, chat spam, music recommendation, fraud, click-through rate, cookies, satellite archaeology).
Task types from p.197 (binary, multiclass, multilabel classification, regression).
Generalization as a property of the data, from chapter 5.

summary:
This page closes subsection 6.1.1 (*Framing the problem*) and opens 6.1.2 (*Collecting a dataset*).

After your research you should know your **inputs**, your **targets**, and the **broad task type**. The authors stress that this framing hides two **hypotheses**:

1. your targets *can* be predicted from your inputs, and
2. the data you have (or will collect) is *sufficiently informative* to learn that input-target relationship.

Until a working model exists, both are just hypotheses "waiting to be validated or invalidated." Having examples of X and Y does not mean X contains enough information to predict Y. The example is **stock prediction from recent price history**: you are unlikely to succeed, because price history carries little predictive information.

A sidebar, **Note on ethics**, looks at a project such as "building an AI that rates the trustworthiness of someone from a picture of their face." The authors reject it on two grounds. First, **validity**: there is no clear reason trustworthiness would show on a face. Second, **ethics**: the labels would just record the annotators' biases. A model trained on them would encode those biases in a black box that gives them "a thin veneer of legitimacy," because "the AI algorithm said" sounds more objective than "John Smith said," even though the model is only a learned approximation of John Smith. Such a model would be "laundering and operationalizing at scale" bad human judgment. The sidebar ends: *technology is never neutral; technical choices are also ethical choices.*

Section **6.1.2** then calls data collection "the most arduous, time-consuming, and costly part of most machine learning projects" and starts going through the example projects. The **photo search engine** needs a label set (10,000 common categories) and manual tagging of hundreds of thousands of past user uploads. The **chat spam detector** cannot train on user chats because they are end-to-end encrypted, so it needs a separate dataset (this continues on p.199).

paragraphs.excerpt: Once you’ve done your research, you should know what your inputs will be,
paragraphs.what_it_says: By the end of the framing stage you should know three things: the inputs, the targets, and the broad type of ML task. You should also be aware of the hypotheses you are making at this point.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This sums up subsection 6.1.1. The questions on p.196-197 (what is the data, what do we predict, what task type is it) should now have answers. The authors then ask you to be suspicious of those answers: committing to a framing means committing to assumptions that have not been tested yet.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Practitioners often treat the framing as settled once it is written down. Calling its assumptions hypotheses keeps you open to finding out later that the project cannot work as framed.
paragraphs.technical_idea: A framing is a choice of input space X, target space Y and loss/task family. Learning then looks for a function f: X -> Y within a hypothesis space, which only makes sense if some useful f exists.

terminology.meaning: The data the model receives (X) and the values it must produce (Y).
The category of ML problem (binary classification, multiclass, regression, etc.) listed on p.197.

connections: p.197: the list of task-type questions and their answers for each example project.
p.196: the framing questions (why is the customer solving this, what data is available).

paragraphs.excerpt: You hypothesize that your targets can be predicted given your inputs.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The first hypothesis: the targets are predictable from the inputs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is a claim about the world, not about your dataset: there has to be a real dependency between X and Y. If Y is essentially independent of X, no amount of data or modeling will help.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the most basic way a project can fail, and you cannot rule it out before you try. A model that beats a baseline (p.205) is the first evidence that it holds.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in statistical terms, Y must have nonzero mutual information with X; otherwise the best possible predictor is the constant that minimizes the loss over the marginal distribution of Y.

terminology.meaning: Here an unverified assumption about the problem, not the 'hypothesis space' of a model.

connections: p.205: beating a baseline is how you first show that X has predictive power.

paragraphs.excerpt: You hypothesize that the data that’s available (or that you will soon collect)
paragraphs.what_it_says: The second hypothesis: the data you have (or will collect) is informative enough to learn the input-target relationship.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Even if Y depends on X in principle, your particular dataset may be too small, too noisy, badly labeled or unrepresentative to reveal that dependency. This hypothesis is about the data you actually have, not about the world.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why the following subsections (6.1.2 collecting data, 'Beware of nonrepresentative data' on p.200, 6.1.3 understanding data on p.202) matter so much: they are how you make the second hypothesis more likely to hold.

terminology.meaning: Containing enough signal (quantity, label quality, relevant features, representativeness) for a model to learn the mapping.

connections: p.199: generalization comes almost entirely from properties of the training data.
p.200: nonrepresentative data is a common way this hypothesis fails.

paragraphs.excerpt: Until you have a working model, these are merely hypotheses, waiting to be
paragraphs.what_it_says: Both hypotheses stay unverified until a model works. Not every problem can be solved with ML: having X and Y examples does not mean X contains enough information to predict Y. Predicting a stock's movements from its recent price history will probably fail, because that history contains little predictive information.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Machine learning is not magic. It can only extract information that is already in the inputs. The stock example is a well-known case: in a fairly efficient market, past prices are already priced in, so whatever signal they carry is close to noise.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets expectations for clients and for yourself. A failed model may be telling you the truth about the problem, not showing that your engineering was poor.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): this is the gap between the irreducible (Bayes) error of a problem and what your model achieves. If the Bayes error for 'up vs. down tomorrow given past prices' is close to 50%, no model can do much better than a coin flip.

terminology.meaning: The part of the input that actually reduces uncertainty about the target.

connections: p.28: machine learning needs input data, expected outputs and a way to measure performance, but these alone do not guarantee learnability.

paragraphs.excerpt: You may sometimes be offered ethically dubious projects, such as “building an AI
paragraphs.what_it_says: Sidebar, first paragraph. A project that rates trustworthiness from a face photo fails twice. Its validity is doubtful because there is no clear reason trustworthiness would show on a face, and it is ethically fraught because the labels would capture annotators' biases. A model trained on them would encode those biases in a black box with a veneer of legitimacy. In a tech-illiterate society, 'the AI said so' carries more weight than 'John Smith said so,' even though the AI is only an approximation of John Smith's judgment. The model would launder and scale the worst of human judgment and hurt real people.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The argument ties ethics to the two hypotheses above. The first objection is an ML objection: the first hypothesis (targets predictable from inputs) is implausible. The second objection explains what the model would learn instead. With no real signal, it would learn the only consistent pattern in the labels, which is the labelers' prejudices. Supervised learning approximates whatever function produced the labels, so if people produced the labels, the model reproduces those people.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows that a model's output can seem objective without being so. Automating a biased judgment does not remove the bias. It hides it and applies it to far more people.
paragraphs.technical_idea: A supervised model approximates p(label | input) as defined by the labeling process. If the labels come from subjective human judgment, the 'ground truth' is that judgment, and the model can at best match it.

terminology.meaning: A surface appearance of objectivity that a judgment gets from being produced by an algorithm.
Passing biased human judgments through a model so they come out looking neutral.
Turning a judgment into an automated process applied to large numbers of people.

connections: p.198 (main text): the first hypothesis, that targets are predictable from inputs, is exactly what fails here.

paragraphs.excerpt: Technology is never neutral. If your work has any impact on the world,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Sidebar, second paragraph. Technology is never neutral. Work that has an impact has a moral direction, technical choices are ethical choices, and you should be deliberate about the values your work supports.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors reject the idea that engineers only build tools and bear no responsibility for how they are used. Choosing which tasks to accept, which data to collect and what to optimize are all value-laden decisions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The workflow chapter is about real-world projects, and here the authors make ethical judgment part of defining the task, before any data is collected.

terminology.meaning: The idea that the effects of a piece of technology are good or bad for people, not neutral.

paragraphs.excerpt: Once you understand the nature of the task and you know what your
paragraphs.what_it_says: Once the task, inputs and targets are understood, data collection begins. The authors call it the most arduous, time-consuming and costly part of most ML projects.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Earlier chapters used ready-made datasets from keras.datasets (p.196 notes you won't have that luxury in practice). In real projects someone has to gather the raw data and, usually, label it by hand.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shifts where you expect to spend time and money. The next page argues that extra hours are usually better spent on more data than on model tweaks.

terminology.meaning: Gathering raw inputs and, for supervised learning, their target annotations.

connections: p.196: 'It would be very convenient if you could import the correct dataset from keras.datasets…'
p.199: the 'Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data' discussion.

paragraphs.excerpt: The photo search engine project requires you to first select the set of
paragraphs.what_it_says: For the photo search engine you first choose a label vocabulary (10,000 common image categories), then manually tag hundreds of thousands of past user-uploaded images with labels from it.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Labeling is two jobs. You design the label set (a taxonomy decision that defines what the model can ever output), then you annotate (repetitive human work). Because the task is multilabel (p.197), each image can get several tags, which makes annotation slower.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a sense of the scale involved: 10,000 classes and hundreds of thousands of images means a large annotation effort, often done with crowdsourcing or annotation tools.

terminology.meaning: The fixed list of categories the classifier can predict.
Humans assigning labels to examples to produce training targets.

connections: p.197: the photo search engine is framed as multiclass, multilabel classification.

paragraphs.excerpt: For the chat app spam detection project, because user chats are end-to-end
paragraphs.what_it_says: For the chat spam detector, user chats are end-to-end encrypted, so their contents cannot be used for training. You need another source (the sentence continues on p.199: tens of thousands of unfiltered social media posts, tagged by hand as spam, offensive or acceptable).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Privacy and legal constraints can rule out the most obvious data source. You then have to use a proxy dataset that, ideally, resembles production traffic.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is an early hint of the representativeness problem on p.200: a proxy dataset may differ from what the deployed model will see.

terminology.meaning: Only the communicating users can read messages, so the service operator, and therefore its training pipeline, cannot.
Data from a related source used because the target-domain data is unavailable.

concepts.name: The two framing hypotheses
concepts.definition: When you frame an ML task you implicitly assume (1) targets can be predicted from inputs and (2) your available data is informative enough to learn that relationship.
concepts.intuition: Before building, you are betting that the signal exists and that your data captures it.
concepts.technical: Hypothesis 1 is about the joint distribution p(X, Y): Y must depend on X. Hypothesis 2 is about the finite sample: its size, label noise and coverage must allow a learner to approximate that dependency.
concepts.significance: Both are only confirmed by a working model. This is why the workflow later asks you to beat a baseline first.
concepts.example: Stock moves from past prices: hypothesis 1 likely fails. A great idea trained on 50 mislabeled examples: hypothesis 2 fails.
concepts.misconception: Having inputs and labels does not mean the problem is learnable.

concepts.name: Predictive information in inputs
concepts.definition: The amount of information the inputs carry about the target; ML can only use what is present.
concepts.intuition: A model can't read tomorrow's price in yesterday's chart if it isn't there.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: formally related to mutual information I(X;Y) and to the Bayes error rate, the lowest error any predictor can reach.
concepts.significance: Sets an upper bound on achievable performance regardless of architecture.
concepts.example: The book's stock-market example: recent price history 'doesn't contain much predictive information.'
concepts.misconception: A bigger model can't create signal that isn't in the inputs.

concepts.name: Label bias / bias laundering
concepts.definition: When labels encode human prejudice, a model trained on them reproduces that prejudice while appearing objective.
concepts.intuition: The model is a learned copy of the annotators; dressing their opinion up as 'AI' doesn't change what it is.
concepts.technical: Supervised learning fits the conditional distribution that generated the labels; if that process is biased, the optimum is biased.
concepts.significance: Central to the book's ethics sidebar; it explains why some projects should be refused.
concepts.example: A face-based 'trustworthiness' rater trained on human ratings learns the raters' stereotypes.
concepts.misconception: 'The algorithm decided' does not mean the decision is neutral.

concepts.name: Data collection and annotation
concepts.definition: Acquiring raw inputs and producing their targets (often by manual labeling); the book calls it the most arduous, time-consuming and costly part of most ML projects.
concepts.intuition: The model is cheap; the textbook-quality dataset behind it is not.
concepts.technical: Includes designing the label taxonomy, sourcing data under legal/privacy constraints, and annotating at scale.
concepts.significance: Data quality and quantity largely determine generalization (p.199).
concepts.example: 10,000 categories and hundreds of thousands of images for the photo search engine.
concepts.misconception: Real projects rarely start from a ready-made dataset like those in keras.datasets.

deeper.title: Why stock prediction from prices is so hard
deeper.body: Beyond the book: the *efficient market hypothesis* holds that public information, including past prices, is quickly reflected in the current price. If it holds even approximately, the next move given past prices is close to a random walk. Any pattern that did predict returns would be exploited by traders until it disappeared. In this book's terms, the first framing hypothesis (targets predictable from inputs) fails because the data generating process actively removes the signal.

deeper.title: Two hypotheses, two kinds of failure
deeper.body:
- **Hypothesis 1 fails** (no signal in X): validation performance stays at baseline whatever you do. More data won't help; you need different inputs.
- **Hypothesis 2 fails** (signal exists but your data is weak): performance may improve with more or cleaner data, better coverage or better labels. The book's advice on p.199 to spend extra hours on data addresses this case.

Note (not in the book): telling these apart in practice is hard. Learning curves (performance vs. dataset size) help. If performance is still rising as you add data, hypothesis 2 is the bottleneck.

deeper.title: The model as a mirror of its labelers
deeper.body: Think of a photocopier that makes a million copies of one person's handwritten opinion, typeset in an official-looking font. The copies look authoritative, but the content is unchanged. The book makes this point: the model is "a learned approximation" of John Smith, yet it is trusted more than John Smith.

misconceptions.claim: If I can assemble pairs of inputs and targets, a deep enough network will learn to predict the targets.
misconceptions.correction: The book is explicit: having X and Y doesn't mean X contains enough information to predict Y (e.g., stock prices from price history).

misconceptions.claim: An algorithm's judgment is more objective than a human's.
misconceptions.correction: A model trained on human labels is a learned approximation of those humans; it inherits their biases and only appears more objective.

misconceptions.claim: Most of an ML project's effort goes into designing the model.
misconceptions.correction: The book calls data collection the most arduous, time-consuming and costly part of most projects.

misconceptions.claim: Technology is a neutral tool; ethics is someone else's job.
misconceptions.correction: The sidebar states that technology is never neutral and technical choices are also ethical choices.

takeaways: Framing a task implies two hypotheses: targets are predictable from inputs, and your data is informative enough to learn that mapping.
These hypotheses are only validated by a working model; not every problem is solvable with ML (e.g., stock moves from past prices).
Models trained on biased human labels reproduce those biases with a false aura of objectivity; some projects are invalid and harmful.
Technical choices are ethical choices; be deliberate about the values your work supports.
Data collection and annotation is usually the most arduous, time-consuming and costly part of an ML project.

questions.question: What are the two hypotheses the book says you make once you know your inputs, targets and task type?
questions.answer: (1) Your targets can be predicted given your inputs; (2) the available (or soon-collected) data is sufficiently informative to learn the relationship between inputs and targets.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets at the top of the page; the book stresses they remain hypotheses until you have a working model.

questions.question: Why does the book say predicting stock movements from recent price history is unlikely to succeed?
options: Stock data is too large to fit in memory
Price history doesn't contain much predictive information
Deep learning cannot handle time series
There are not enough labeled examples of stock prices
questions.answer: Price history doesn't contain much predictive information
questions.explanation: The book's reason is that the inputs lack predictive information, a failure of the first hypothesis. Size is not the issue, later chapters do handle time series, and price data is plentiful and self-labeling.

questions.question: The ethics sidebar gives two objections to a face-based trustworthiness rater. How does the first objection relate to the two hypotheses on the same page?
questions.answer: The first objection (validity: no clear reason trustworthiness would show on a face) says hypothesis 1, that targets are predictable from inputs, is implausible. With no real signal, the model would only learn the labelers' biases.
questions.explanation: This connects the ML-validity argument to the ethical one: when the true signal is absent, the only learnable pattern in the labels is the labelers' prejudice.

questions.question: Why can't the chat app's own messages be used to train the spam detector?
questions.answer: User chats are end-to-end encrypted, so their contents can't be used; a separate dataset must be obtained and labeled.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last bullet; p.199 completes it with tens of thousands of social media posts tagged as spam, offensive or acceptable.

questions.question: According to the book, which part of most ML projects is the most arduous, time-consuming and costly?
questions.explanation: The opening sentence of 6.1.2 says this directly. The other steps matter, but the book singles out data collection.

questions.question: Why does the book say 'The AI algorithm said this person cannot be trusted' is not more objective than 'John Smith said this person cannot be trusted'?
questions.answer: Because the model is a learned approximation of human labelers like John Smith; it encodes their judgments and biases, just in a black box that looks more legitimate.
questions.explanation: Supervised learning approximates the labeling function. If people provide the labels, the model approximates those people.

questions.question: Pick a project you'd like to build. Write down your inputs, targets and task type, then judge how confident you are in each of the two hypotheses, and whether the project raises any ethical concerns.
questions.answer: Answers vary; a good answer identifies a concrete reason to believe the signal exists and the data captures it, plus any bias or harm risks.
questions.explanation: This applies the page's checklist (framing, hypotheses, ethics) to your own work before you spend effort on data collection.
